title: The resentment list

lines: HE ABUSED ME, HE ROBBED ME.
WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO RECITES IT.
cards: "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." That's not a police report. It's the third verse of the Dhammapada, the Buddhist collection of sayings, in Max Müller's translation.
It sounds like something the mind says at night, on a loop, about a boss or a sibling or an ex: a list, recited from memory, item by item. The verse isn't asking anyone to pretend the list is false.
It's pointing at what happens to the one who keeps reciting it. Today: the resentment list.

teach.b: First, the verse finishes its sentence: "in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." The next verse repeats the same list and says that in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease.
The list is identical. What changes is harboring: keeping it docked, tied up and fed. Second, why paper helps.
A list in your head never ends, because the mind keeps adding and repeating.

teach.h: A LIST ON PAPER HAS EDGES.
teach.b: A list on paper has edges. You can see there are five things, not five hundred, and that some are old and small. Alcoholics Anonymous makes a written practice of this.
Its Big Book describes writing resentments down: who you resent, what happened, and what it touched in you. Then the uncomfortable part: an honest look at your own share, where there is one.
Not to excuse anyone, but to see the whole picture.
Third, a warning from the letter to the Hebrews: "lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled." A root works underground; you don't see it until it has spread.
Writing the list digs it up into daylight, where it can be looked at instead of growing in the dark. Fourth, honesty.
The list only works if it's true, petty ones included, the ones you'd be embarrassed to say aloud.
Nobody grades it. The page can hold the same list the Dhammapada quotes, without the harboring.

how: In Alcoholics Anonymous, members often write a resentment inventory with a sponsor's help, listing whom they resent, why, and what it affected, and then looking at their own part.

games.q: you're writing your resentment list. one item feels too petty and embarrassing to put down. what do you do?
o: leave it off; it's beneath you.
write it down with the others.
write a more dignified version of it.
games.why: the list only works if it's true. the petty ones loop in the head just as hard as the big ones.

practice: On a page, write three resentments, one per line: a name or a place, and in a few words what happened.
Beside each, write what it touched, your pride, your money, your safety, your sense of being loved, and, if you're willing, whether any part of it was yours.
Then look at the page for a few breaths, and notice that there are three lines, and that they stop.
